story.title: Supreme Court Considers Catholic Schools' Participation in Colorado Preschool Program
story.summary: The Supreme Court is deliberating a case involving Catholic preschools in Colorado that seek to join the state's universal preschool program. The schools argue that their exclusion based on their admissions policy, which does not accept families with gay and transgender parents, is unconstitutional. The court appears to be sympathetic to the Catholic schools' position regarding potential exemptions from Colorado's anti-discrimination rules for taxpayer-funded programs.

explore_lenses.label: What is the legal issue before the Court?
explore_lenses.title: Whether Colorado may attach this condition to funding
explore_lenses.summary: The case concerns whether Colorado may require participating preschools—including religious ones—to comply with its equal-enrollment rule as a condition of receiving Universal Preschool funds. The Supreme Court accepted two questions about Free Exercise doctrine, not the petitioners’ separate request to overrule a 1990 precedent outright.

claims.text: Colorado law requires every participating preschool provider to give eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive services regardless of characteristics including religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, income, disability, and those characteristics as applied to a child’s family.

The Catholic preschools argue that Colorado permits comparable secular enrollment preferences—for example, preferences connected to income or disability—but refuses an accommodation for their religious admissions practices.
Colorado’s position is that the other permitted admissions decisions comply with, rather than conflict with, its nondiscrimination rules.

The Court granted review only on questions concerning when secular exemptions or discretion make a rule insufficiently generally applicable, and how its Carson v. Makin precedent applies; it did not grant review on whether Employment Division v. Smith should be overruled.

explore_lenses.label: How did this reach the Supreme Court?
explore_lenses.title: A 2023 program dispute moved through the Tenth Circuit
explore_lenses.summary: The dispute began after Colorado launched its UPK program and the Archdiocese chose not to enroll its parish preschools under the nondiscrimination condition. The federal appeals court upheld Colorado’s policy in 2025, after which the Supreme Court granted review in April 2026.

claims.text: Colorado implemented UPK in 2023 as a mixed-delivery program in which public, private, religious, and nonreligious providers can be reimbursed for serving eligible children.

According to the Tenth Circuit, the Archdiocese instructed its preschools not to register for UPK in 2023 rather than agree to the nondiscrimination requirement; it had sought a faith-based-provider exemption from state officials.
The Tenth Circuit issued a published decision affirming the judgment for Colorado on September 30, 2025.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari on April 20, 2026, limited to two of the petitioners’ three proposed questions.

explore_lenses.label: What could the ruling change?
explore_lenses.title: It could shape funding rules for religious providers
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate result will determine whether these Catholic preschools can participate in Colorado UPK without accepting the contested enrollment condition. The broader significance turns on how the Court defines the state’s ability to attach nondiscrimination conditions to generally available public-benefit programs.

claims.text: The program at issue funds preschool selected by parents at public or private schools, while participation requires providers to meet the state’s equal-opportunity enrollment condition.

The preschools and the Archdiocese say exclusion forces families seeking Catholic preschool to pay privately and amounts to unequal treatment of religious institutions in an otherwise available benefit program.
Colorado contends that a provider’s refusal to admit children from LGBTQ+ families conflicts with the state’s antidiscrimination requirement.
Forecast: AP reports that a ruling for the preschools could further narrow Employment Division v. Smith, the 1990 precedent governing religious-exemption claims against generally applicable laws.

story_report.summary: The Supreme Court has heard a challenge by Catholic preschools seeking to join Colorado’s state-funded universal preschool program while maintaining admissions practices that the state says conflict with its protections for LGBTQ+ families. The justices are reviewing a lower-court ruling for Colorado and have limited the case to questions about religious exemptions and the application of prior Free Exercise precedent. No decision has been issued, leaving the schools’ participation in the program unresolved.

sections.heading: Colorado Universal Preschool Program
sections.body: Colorado launched its universal preschool program in 2023 as a mixed-delivery system that reimburses public, private, religious and nonreligious providers for serving eligible children. Parents may select participating public or private schools, but providers must meet the state’s equal-opportunity enrollment condition. State law requires participating providers to give eligible children equal access regardless of characteristics including religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, income and disability, including as those characteristics apply to a child’s family.

sections.heading: Religious Exemption and Enrollment Rules
sections.body: The Archdiocese and its preschools contend that Colorado allows comparable secular enrollment preferences, including ones related to income or disability, while declining to accommodate their religious admissions practices. Colorado’s position is that those other decisions comply with its nondiscrimination rules, whereas refusing to admit children from LGBTQ+ families conflicts with them. According to the Tenth Circuit, the Archdiocese told its preschools not to register in 2023 rather than accept the requirement after seeking a faith-based-provider exemption.

sections.heading: Supreme Court Review Scope
sections.body: The Supreme Court granted review of two questions concerning when secular exemptions or official discretion can make a rule insufficiently generally applicable, and how Carson v. Makin applies. It did not agree to review whether Employment Division v. Smith should be overruled. A ruling for the preschools could further narrow Smith’s framework for religious-exemption claims against generally applicable laws, according to an AP forecast cited in the evidence packet.

unresolved.text: The Court has not issued an opinion. Its eventual ruling could be limited to Colorado’s program structure or establish a broader Free Exercise rule, and the scope will depend on the opinion’s reasoning and vote alignment.

related_stories.title: Russian Airstrikes on Ukrainian Aid Center Result in 31 Deaths and Many Missing
related_stories.summary: A Russian bombing raid on a humanitarian aid center in the village of Komyshuvakha, located in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, has resulted in at least 31 fatalities. Emergency teams are searching through the debris, with more than 45 residents reported missing. The attack involved the use of large aerial bombs and is part of a broader wave of strikes across Ukraine, which also targeted power plants and hospitals.
